paper.title: IL-13 driven tuft cell hyperplasia is suppressed by retinoic acid in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.
paper.abstract: Tuft cells are specialized chemosensory epithelial cells that contribute to mucosal immunity, yet how their differentiation is regulated in human airway disease remains unclear. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps(CRSwNP) features type 2 inflammation and expansion of sinonasal tuft cells, consistent with type 2 cytokine-driven epithelial remodeling. Using primary human sinonasal epithelial air-liquid interface cultures, we examined tuft cell differentiation across disease phenotypes. IL-13-induced expansion of POU2F3+ tuft cells and generated a BMX+ subset consistent with a mature or activated phenotype. These IL-13 activated cultures exhibited enhanced responsiveness to chemosensory ligands such as succinate and denatonium, indicating functional activation. Surprisingly, IL-13-driven sinonasal tuft cell differentiation occurred despite inhibition of STAT6 and ERK signaling, suggesting involvement of noncanonical pathways. Retinoic acid(RA) emerged as a selective regulator of tuft cell differentiation specifically in CRSwNP. RA did not alter STAT6 phosphorylation or canonical IL-13-responsive gene expression, indicating that RA suppresses tuft cell differentiation through distinct mechanisms. These findings highlight a noncanonical pathway of IL-13-mediated tuft cell expansion and identify retinoic acid as a context-dependent regulator of tuft cell differentiation in the airway. These findings demonstrate methods to regulate human sinonasal tuft cell differentiation across disease phenotypes, opening avenues for tuft cell-targeted therapeutic strategies.

paper.title: Food-Derived l-tryptophan and α-Casein (90-95) Differentially Potentiate Porcine Calcium-Sensing Receptor Signaling and Improve Enteroendocrine-Epithelial Responses Under Peptidoglycan Challenge.
paper.abstract: The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a nutrient-sensing class C G protein-coupled receptor implicated in intestinal hormone release, yet the signaling pharmacology of the porcine receptor and its relevance to epithelial homeostasis remain poorly defined. Here, a stable Flp-In-293 reporter platform expressing porcine CaSR was combined with structure-based docking, molecular dynamics simulations, secretin tumor cell line-1 (STC-1) enteroendocrine assays, and an STC-1/IPEC-J2 co-culture system challenged with peptidoglycan. Extracellular Ca2+ activated porcine CaSR through NFAT, SRE, SRF, and cAMP readouts, whereas l-tryptophan and α-casein (90-95) differentially potentiated Ca2+-dependent signaling and docked within the extracellular Venus flytrap domain. Both ligands stimulated CaSR-sensitive glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) secretion and recruited ERK1/2, IP1, and cAMP signaling. In co-culture, ligand exposure attenuated inflammatory transcription, preserved selected transporter and tight-junction programs, and improved barrier function under peptidoglycan challenge. Together, these data identify food-derived ligands that couple porcine CaSR signaling to enteroendocrine-epithelial responses.

paper.title: Rapid nasal metabolism organizes the neural representation of odors.
paper.abstract: The olfactory system translates chemical stimuli (odorants) into neural patterns of activity that give rise to odor perception. Canonical models of odor coding consider the binding of odorants to receptors expressed on olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) as the primary organizing step in this process1. However, such models fail to account for key aspects of odorant-evoked responses measured in vivo. Here, we considered how a process peripheral to receptor-ligand binding - the metabolism of odorants by xenobiotic enzymes in the nasal mucosa - may impact odor codes in vivo. Using imaging in awake mice and odorants linked by well-characterized enzymatic pathways2-4, we find that nasal metabolism rapidly generates odorous metabolites and profoundly alters odor representations over a time-scale relevant for odor perception. Rapid odorant metabolism explains what otherwise appears to be complex tuning of OSNs as well as diverse temporal response patterns not accounted for by a simple receptor-ligand model. While nasal metabolism introduces confusion between identity-based representations of inhaled versus metabolism-generated odorants, we find that inhalation-linked response timing resolves this confusion and that temporally segregated representations of inhaled versus metabolism-generated odorants are preserved at the level of olfactory bulb projections to cortex. These findings demonstrate that odorant metabolism is integral to olfactory sensation and define a novel role for timing in olfaction: to distinguish external chemical signals from those generated internally, potentially supporting distinct percepts and behavioral responses to each.

paper.title: TRPA1-associated attenuation of AITC-evoked pungency in acidic wasabi sauces: Sensory, cellular and in silico insights.
paper.abstract: Wasabi and mustard sauces derive their characteristic pungency from allyl isothiocyanate (AITC), which elicits a sharp, irritating sensation by activating the transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) ion channel in sensory neurons. It is observed that in diverse culinary forms, AITC consistently exists within acidic matrices that exhibit noticeable sour tastes. However, few studies have been carried out on the influence of such acidic environments on AITC-induced pungency. We characterized eight commercial wasabi and mustard products using GC-MS and ion chromatography, revealing that AITC was the major pungent component in wasabi samples but was present at low levels or undetectable in mustard products (pH range: 3.0-5.0). Sensory evaluations (n = 13 participants) revealed that acidified mustard oil emulsions at pH 4 significantly reduced oral pungency ratings compared to neutral pH (mean scores: 4.9 ± 0.5 vs. 6.8 ± 0.4, p < 0.05 on a 1-9 scale). Consistently, cellular assays using TRPA1-overexpressing HEK293T cells demonstrated that acidification to pH 4 markedly reduced the cellular response to AITC compared to pH 7. Similarly, in hiPSC-derived sensory neurons, acidic pH reduced AITC-evoked neuronal firing activity Using AlphaFold 3, molecular docking and dynamics simulations provide preliminary insights suggesting that acidification may induce noticeable dynamic perturbations, including recurring oscillations in radius of gyration (Rg), a late-stage surge in root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), and sustained elevation of solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). These dynamic features collectively suggest a tendency toward destabilization of the TRPA1-AITC complex under acidic condition, which is consistent with the diminished channel activation and lower pungency perception. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into a potential mechanism by which food matrix acidity may modulate TRPA1 activity, offering a tentative scientific basis for the formulation of pungent foods with reduced irritancy.

paper.title: Neuroepigenetic programming by the maternal environment: part A-epigenome-wide DNA methylation profile in the offspring's olfactory bulb following preconceptional weight loss in mice.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Experimental models and epidemiological data suggest that the maternal nutritional environment during gestation plays important roles in brain development with consequences on cognitive health. Epigenetic marks, such as methylation and histone modifications, are likely to be involved in this programming, but little addressed the impact of maternal metabolism at the preconceptional period. In mice, we recently demonstrated lasting effects of a maternal preconceptional weight loss on metabolic outcomes and behaviors related to food intake in the male offspring, exhibiting a reduction in olfactory sensitivity, along with a lack of fasting-induced olfactory-based motivation. To evaluate if this effect was driven by epigenetic modifications in the olfactory bulb, we profiled brain DNA methylation, a fundamental process in mediating the relation between early life environment and long-term behaviors in mice according to the maternal status.

RESULTS: Using oxidative reduced representation bisulfite sequencing to specifically target 5mC in mice exposed to preconceptional weight loss versus controls, we identified 11,055 differentially methylated cytosines and 150 differential methylated regions (DMRs) located in 111 genes in the olfactory bulb, a main region involved in odor processing and integration. Among the cytosines differentially methylated, half were hypermethylated. Methylation remodeling according to the maternal group preferentially affected noncoding intragenic regions, distal regulatory elements, and open sea CpGs, while promoter CpG islands remain relatively resistant to modification in DNA methylome. The functional annotation of DMRs pointed out genes related to histones kinases, energy signaling, synaptic function, and cellular differentiation, suggesting that targeted methylation changes may simultaneously influence epigenetic regulation, metabolism, and neurobiology.

CONCLUSION: Thanks to a single-base analysis of differential methylated CpGs, we present novel evidence that the maternal dietary environment prior to conception exerts maternally-driven epigenetic effects, markedly altering 5-methylcytosine patterns in the adult offspring brain. This long-lasting remodeling of the offspring's olfactory bulb methylome may underlie the described alterations in olfactory-driven behaviors of offspring born to WL mother.

paper.title: Saliva Selectively Binds to Pungent Odors during Oral Consumption of Durian.
paper.abstract: Durian (Durio zibethinus) is well known for its odoriferous flavor character due to the presence of volatile sulfur compounds. However, its flavor behavior in the oral cavity has not yet been explored. Herein, the in vivo flavor composition of durian during oral processing was characterized, showing that the volatile flavor composition released into the oronasal cavity significantly differs from its headspace composition. It was surprising to observe that only <5 % of the total volatile content released during oral processing reaches the nasal cavity. Moreover, the sulfur-to-ester ratio of volatile components significantly decreases, suggesting that durian flavor may be perceived differently in retronasal versus orthonasal pathways. In vitro simulations further reveal that salivary mucin selectively binds to the sulfur content, changing the eventual volatile composition reaching the olfactory receptors during consumption. These findings hold significant implications toward understanding how oral processing impacts flavor composition and perception through retronasal and orthonasal mechanisms.

paper.title: Role of olfactory receptor Olfr544 in neuronal cells: Insights into neurite outgrowth and CREB signaling.
paper.abstract: Olfactory receptors (ORs) are expressed beyond the nasal epithelium and implicated in brain function, yet their roles remain unclear. This study investigated the function of the OR Olfr544, which has been reported to be highly expressed near amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's disease model mice, using the mouse neuroblastoma N2a cell line. We found that its agonist azelaic acid (AZA) promotes neurite outgrowth and activates the cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling cascade in an Olfr544-dependent manner. Transcriptome analysis of Olfr544-knockout cells revealed altered expression of genes involved in neuroactive signaling and cytoskeletal organization. Key downstream targets, including Igf2bp3, were identified and validated. These results establish a functional link between an extra-olfactory OR and neuronal morphology via CREB in vitro, providing a mechanistic basis for further studies of OR functions in the nervous system.

paper.title: Development-inspired approach for the derivation of functional and transplantable salivary gland organoids from human pluripotent stem cells.
paper.abstract: Salivary gland (SG) hypofunction significantly affects the life quality of patients with hyposalivation. Current treatment options for these conditions are limited and often result in undesirable side effects. To address this issue, we've developed a developmentally inspired strategy to derive salivary gland epithelial progenitor (SGEP) cells from human pluripotent stem cells (PSC). Then we employ SGEP cells derived from human PSC with a SOX10::GFP reporter to engineer three-dimensional lumenized SG organoids, with well-defined lumens and secretory function, reminiscent of human salivary glands. Upon transplantation into the submandibular gland of athymic nude mice, mCherry+ salivary gland organoids (SGO) integrate into the gland and differentiated into salivary gland phenotypes, including acinar, ductal and myoepithelial structures. Our findings suggest that SG organoids may hold promise for studying SG development, disease progression and drug screening, as well as for development of cell therapies for salivary gland regeneration.

paper.title: Long-Chain Fatty Acids Inhibit the Human Bitter Taste Receptor TAS2R16 in a Structure-Dependent Manner.
paper.abstract: Bitterness limits the development of palatable foods containing bioactive ingredients. This study investigated whether long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) modulate the human bitter taste receptor TAS2R16 using a HEK293T cell-based calcium assay with salicin as an agonist. None of the tested LCFAs directly activated TAS2R16. Under co-treatment, only oleic acid inhibited salicin-induced calcium responses, shifting the salicin EC50 from 1.82 ± 0.11 mM to 3.55 ± 1.22 mM at 30 μM (p < 0.01). Pretreatment with all LCFAs inhibited TAS2R16 concentration-dependently. Reliable IC50 values were obtained for palmitic acid (8.67 ± 1.44 μM), stearic acid (0.082 ± 0.002 μM), and oleic acid (0.41 ± 0.12 μM), whereas lower plateaus were not reached for myristic, linoleic, and α-linolenic acids. LCFA treatment did not consistently change membrane fluidity, and inhibition was attenuated in the TAS2R16 N96T mutant. These findings demonstrate compound- and treatment-dependent modulation of TAS2R16 by food-derived LCFAs.

paper.title: NOSE-OE: A molecular signaling map of the olfactory epithelium.
paper.abstract: The olfactory epithelium (OE) is a dynamic and complex sensory tissue in which continuous regeneration, neuronal differentiation, and tissue maintenance depend on coordinated molecular and cellular signaling. We developed NOSE-OE (Network of Signaling Events in the Olfactory Epithelium), an open-access knowledge resource that integrates mechanistic evidence from more than 300 publications into a standardized, computer-readable signaling network. NOSE-OE comprises over 500 molecular elements and 1,000 curated interactions and is implemented within the MINERVA platform for interactive exploration and network analysis. By connecting fragmented experimental evidence within a unified molecular framework, NOSE-OE enables the systematic investigation of signaling processes governing OE homeostasis and responses to perturbation. The resource provides a foundation for hypothesis generation and systems-level investigation of olfactory epithelial biology across physiological and disease contexts.

paper.title: Myelinated mechano-nociceptors encode noxious cold and underlie hypersensitivity in pulpitis.
paper.abstract: The ability to identify dangerous temperatures is critical, but the neural basis for cold sensation remains enigmatic. By combining in vivo functional imaging with tissue-specific spatiotemporal cooling, we unveil myelinated high threshold-mechanonociceptors (HTMRs) as the neural origin of tooth cold sensitivity. Critically, this neural encoding is driven by threshold noxious cold temperature, not cooling rate and remains independent of the cool receptor TRPM8 or pain transducer Nav1.8. Furthermore, while Bmpr1b -Cre captures the intradental HTMRs, it further reveals myelinated HTMRs mediate trigeminal cold encoding in soft tissues. Finally, we determine that inflammation potentiates intradental HTMRs, providing functional basis for clinical hypersensitivity in pulpitis. Collectively, our results reveal a new neural mediator of cold sensation and provide insight into painful transformation of cold sensory encoding in inflammation.

paper.title: TasTY: Development and evaluation of a taste test for quantifying taste sensitivity among preschool children-test-retest reliability, application, and comparison between children with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
paper.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Taste dysfunction gained attention during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic; however, validated objective tests for preschool children remain limited. We aimed to develop a feasible, reliable test quantifying taste sensitivity among children aged 3-6 years and to compare performance between children with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. We included 68 symptom-free children (median age 5.1 years; interquartile range (IQR) 3.9-5.9): 36 without known SARS-CoV-2 infection (control group, CG) and 32 with confirmed prior infection (SARS-CoV-2 infection group, C19-G), tested 79 days after infection (median; IQR 56-112). Children completed a self-developed Taste Test for Young Children (TasTY), a double-blind, playful two-alternative forced-choice test with 10 samples in randomized order (sweet, sour, and salty at three concentrations each; water served as a control). Twenty controls were retested a median of 62 days later (IQR 38-64). Outcomes were total score (0-10), feasibility, task comprehension, and test-retest reliability, assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), standard error of measurement (SEM), and smallest real difference (SRD). Feasibility was high (3% dropout), and 89.4% correctly classified water. Total score test-retest reliability was good (ICC = 0.73; pooled SEM = 0.76; SRD = 2.11). Total scores were similar between CG and C19-G (8.37 ± 1.5 vs. 8.19 ± 1.5; p = 0.63). Descriptively, three-year-olds (n = 17) had lower, more variable scores.

CONCLUSION: TasTY provides an age-appropriate, reliable, objective method for quantifying taste sensitivity among preschoolers, supporting standardized group comparisons and longitudinal assessment.

WHAT IS KNOWN: • COVID-19 increased awareness of taste dysfunction; however, evidence among young children relies mainly on surveys and parental reports. • Objective taste tests for preschool children remain limited.

WHAT IS NEW: • TasTY is a feasible, standardized, and objective test for quantifying taste sensitivity among children aged 3-6 years and goes beyond parental and subjective reports. • Its standardized 0-10 score showed good test-retest reliability and may support group comparisons and longitudinal assessment of preschool children with taste-related conditions.

paper.title: Prevalence of alpha-synuclein seeding activity in the Olfactory Mucosa following SARS-CoV-2 infection: results from a pilot study.
paper.abstract: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is a hallmark of SARS-CoV-2-infection where it is believed to result from neuroinflammation induced by viral invasion via the olfactory mucosa (OM). Hyposmia also affects the majority of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) where it is caused by α-synuclein (aSyn) pathology in the olfactory system, and aSyn-seeding-activity can be detected in the OM using aSyn-seeding-amplification-assays (aSyn-SAA). The present pilot study aimed to investigate whether SARS-CoV-2-infection induces local aSyn-misfolding and -aggregation in OM samples using aSyn-SAA. We conducted an observational study including PD patients (n = 51), individuals with a history of documented symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infection (post-COVID; n = 95), and healthy controls (HC; n = 42). Post-COVID-participants were stratified based on persistent OD (COVID+OD; n = 42) or normal olfaction (COVID-OD; n = 53) using Sniffin'-Sticks-Identification (SSI) and -Discrimination (SSD) tests. OM samples were obtained by ENT specialists and analyzed by aSyn-SAA at the University of Verona. Clinical phenotyping included MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, and the Innsbruck-RBD-Inventory. OM-SAA positivity rates were significantly different between PD and both post-COVID-participants and HCs (80.4% vs 24.2% vs 11.9%; p < 0.001). Within the post-COVID-group, positivity rates were higher in COVID+OD vs COVID-OD (35.7% vs 15.1%; p = 0.030), and COVID+OD differed from HC (p = 0.030), while COVID-OD did not (p = 0.65). Among post-COVID-participants, aSyn-SAA positivity was associated with lower SSI (p = 0.007) and SSD (p < 0.001) scores, but not with MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, or RBD measures. OM-SAA-positivity was enriched among individuals with persistent post-COVID-OD and correlated with olfactory impairment. These findings support the hypothesis that neuroinflammation following SARS-COV-2-infection might promote local aSyn-aggregation. The biological and prognostic relevance of OM-SAA positivity is unknown and needs further prospective investigation.

paper.title: Aging reshapes odor-evoked dynamics in central olfactory circuits.
paper.abstract: Olfactory decline is among the earliest signs of aging and predicts later cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Age-related impairments in odor identification and discrimination implicate central olfactory brain regions in both mice and humans, but it remains unclear where in the processing hierarchy aging alters neural function relating to these cognitive and perceptual deficits. To resolve this, we acquired simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from olfactory bulb (OB) and piriform cortex (PCx) in young and old mice during awake, head-fixed odor presentation, allowing us to probe multiple levels of odor response features within each animal. Our recordings revealed a shift toward greater excitation in both regions and reduced inhibitory neuron activity in PCx. Aging also restructured odor-evoked local field potential (LFP) oscillations within and across regions, with strongly elevated beta power and coherence. Population odor representations were less discriminable in OB, but not in PCx. Thus, our results point to reduced discriminability of OB population odor representations as the clearest neural analog of previously reported discrimination deficits. Single-unit, LFP, and population measures did not collapse onto a single axis using dimensionality reduction, indicating that several partly independent processes reshape the dynamics of odor responses in central olfactory circuits with aging. Together, these findings identify central circuit excitation/inhibition (E/I) and oscillatory imbalances that parallel age-related olfactory dysfunction despite largely preserved odor responsivity.

paper.title: Odor-evoked activity outside canonical areas of olfactory information transmission is visualized by ODORTRAP and modulated by diet-induced obesity.
paper.abstract: Enhanced excitability of output neurons in the olfactory bulb (OB) has been linked to regulation of energy homeostasis. The mechanism by which the olfactory system can drive metabolic state while processing odor information remains elusive yet must depend upon integration and relay to the rest of the brain. Herein, we screened brain-wide neuronal ensembles that preferentially engaged during odor stimulation (referred to as ODORTRAP) utilizing FOSTRAP activity mapping. Mice were exposed to the odor isopropyl tiglate (IPT), a preferred ligand for the olfactory receptor 160, previously shown to be vulnerable to diet-induced obesity. Odor activation resulted in elevated labelling in the olfactory bulb (ODORTRAP) (p < 0.001), as well as in higher olfactory cortices including anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex, and cortical amygdala (p < 0.05). Interestingly, IPT differentially recruited hypothalamic feeding areas, namely the arcuate (ARC), dorsomedial (DMH) and lateral (LH) hypothalamus (p < 0.001), while the ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus and the suprachiasmatic nucleus exhibited no change in ODORTRAP activity (p > 0.05). In mice that were maintained on moderately high-fat (MHF) diets, we discovered that obesity re-models the activation pattern across the brain. Obese mice exhibited loss of ODORTRAP activity in the ARC (p < 0.0001), whereas in the DMH and LH increased baseline activity that obscured any odor-linked neural activity. While IPT activated the nucleus accumbens and medial septum in control mice (p < 0.01), obese mice demonstrated no changes in ODORTRAP activity (p > 0.05). Our study identifies key brain regions linking chemosensation and metabolic state, specifically demonstrating alteration in activity in hypothalamic domains upon obesogenic diet.

paper.title: Genetic variations underlying bitter and sweet taste perception are associated with food and beverage intake habits and taste-modifying behaviors among Dutch adults with a prior myocardial infarction.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Taste perception influences eating behaviors and varies partly based on genetics. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many variants related to bitter, sweet, salt, sour, and umami perception (taste-related variants), but whether these variants inform eating behaviors among patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD) is unknown. This study investigated the associations of taste-related variants with eating behaviors in adults with a prior myocardial infarction (MI) and explored the potential for sex-specific effects.

METHODS: Analyzed, were 4,204 Dutch adults with a prior MI from the Alpha Omega Cohort (60-80 years; 21% female; BMI: 27.7 ± 3.8 kg/m2). We selected 39 taste-related variants identified in prior GWAS and determined their associations with reported intake frequency of 19 food and beverage groups and 7 taste-modifying behaviors (e.g. adding sugar to coffee) using multivariable regression models adjusted for demographic, lifestyle and socioeconomic factors.

MAIN FINDINGS: 32/39 taste-related variants were nominally (p < 0.05) associated with at least one food or beverage group or taste-modifying behavior, of which 6 passed Bonferroni adjustment (p < 0.05/19 or 0.05/7, respectively). paper.title: Dynamics of Ligand Binding Sites and Chloride Penetration in a Bitter Taste GPCR.
paper.abstract: Taste perception strongly influences food choice, drug compliance, and dietary behavior. Apo simulations without G protein showed shorter-lived chloride visits to the same region. paper.title: Association between central sensitization inventory and taste alterations in patients with burning mouth syndrome: a cross-sectional study.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a chronic condition characterized by a burning sensation in the mouth without observable lesions, lasting over two hours daily for more than three months. In this study, we aimed to examine whether central sensitization inventory (CSI) scores differ between primary and secondary BMS (SBMS), arising from identifiable causes, and to explore their associations with taste thresholds and pain characteristics.

METHODS: This study was conducted between February 2022 and September 2025 and included 30 patients with BMS, 30 patients with SBMS, and 30 healthy controls. Taste assessments, including sweet, salty, sour, and bitter solutions and CSI evaluations, were performed. Statistical analyses, including correlation and comparison tests, were performed using the SPSS software.

RESULTS: Patients with BMS exhibited significantly larger pain visual analog scale (VAS) and CSI scores than those with SBMS. There were no significant differences in taste perception thresholds for the four flavors among the three groups. CSI scores showed significant positive correlations with taste thresholds for sweetness, saltiness, and bitterness in the BMS group, whereas no such correlations were observed in the SBMS group. The pain VAS scores in the BMS group were positively correlated with age and CSI scores. Receiver operating characteristic analysis revealed acceptable CSI discrimination for distinguishing BMS from SBMS (Area under the curve = 0.76). A cutoff of 27 yielded 70% sensitivity and 77% specificity, with an overall accuracy of 73%.

CONCLUSIONS: Although no significant differences in taste thresholds were observed among the three groups, significant associations between the CSI scores and taste thresholds were identified exclusively in patients with BMS. While CSI scores do not directly assess central sensitization, they might reflect clinical features associated with central sensitization-related symptom burden in BMS, as observed for taste thresholds, pain intensity, and age. These findings suggest that taste alterations in BMS might be associated with central sensitization-related clinical features.

paper.title: Effects of endoscopic sinus surgery on clinical outcomes, nasal patency, and olfactory function in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) on treatment efficacy, nasal patency, and olfactory function in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS).

METHODS: A total of 225 patients with CRS admitted to Tianjin Huanhu Hospital were selected. The control group comprised 100 patients who underwent intranasal maxillary antrostomy, while the observation group included 125 patients who underwent endoscopic sinus surgery. Data were collected from both groups were compared, including treatment efficacy, symptom resolution, nasal patency (nasal minimum cross-sectional area (NMCA), nasal airway resistance (NAR), nasal cavity volume (NCV)), nasal mucociliary function (mucociliary clearance velocity and clearance rate), endoscopic findings (Lund-Kennedy score) and olfactory function, serum inflammatory markers (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [hs-CRP], tumor necrosis factor α [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6]), postoperative complications, quality of life using the Chinese version of the Sino-Nasal Outcomes Test 20 [SNOT-20], and short-term recurrence (6-month and 12-month recurrence rates). In addition, the correlation between inflammatory markers and symptom recovery was evaluated.

RESULTS: The observation group demonstrated a significantly higher total effective rate, greater improvements in symptom resolution, mucociliary function, endoscopic findings, olfactory function, and quality of life, than the control group. Both groups showed comparable improvement in nasal patency indices. Serum inflammatory markers, the overall complication rate, and 6- and 12-month recurrence rates were significantly lower in the observation group than in the control group. Correlation analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between Δhs-CRP and olfactory dysfunction (r = 0.156, P = 0.019), and between ΔIL-6 and nasal obstruction (r = 0.175, P = 0.008); however, the clinical relevance of these correlations was limited.

CONCLUSION: ESS provides reliable therapeutic benefits for patients with CRS and merits broader clinical adoption.

paper.title: Bitter 2,5-Diketopiperazines From Cocoa Activate Human Bitter Taste Receptors.
paper.abstract: The human taste system enables a rapid analysis of nutritional and non-nutritional food constituents. Although a bitter taste is considered a warning signal against ingesting potentially harmful substances, not all bitter substances are toxic, and a moderate bitterness is frequently tolerated or even preferred. An important class of bitter compounds found in thermally treated foods is the 2,5-diketopiperazines, cyclic dipeptides made from two L-amino acids, which are frequently formed as degradation products of polypeptides. Although 2,5-diketopiperazines are established as major contributors to the bitter taste of many food items, it is still unknown which of the human bitter taste receptors mediate their detection. Using functional calcium-mobilization assays, we identified two human bitter taste receptors, TAS2R14 and TAS2R43, being responsive to 2,5-diketopiperazines. Of the two identified 2,5-diketopiperazines activating TAS2R43, cis-cyclo(L-Leu-L-Phe) exhibited the highest potency with a threshold concentration of 100 µM. Further testing of 2,5-diketopiperazine-related linear dipeptides revealed that 2,5-diketopiperazines represent their own class of bitter compounds, as no overlapping activation patterns with the corresponding dipeptides were evident.

paper.title: Predicting taste alteration in head and neck cancer patients using 3D transformer-based deep learning model.
paper.abstract:
PURPOSE: Taste alteration is a common post-treatment side effect of head and neck cancer (HNC) radiotherapy. Accurate normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models can support treatment planning aimed at reducing side effects that impair quality-of-life. Deep learning (DL) offers opportunities to incorporate full 3D dose, CT, and organofinterest (OOI) data. Using a large prospective cohort, this study explores whether CNN and transformerbased DL models can outperform a conventional logistic regression model for predicting taste alteration 6 months after radiotherapy.

MATERIAL/METHODS: Data from 972 patients was used, with the endpoint being moderatetosevere patientreported taste alteration at six months (EORTC QLQH&N35). DL models were trained using 3D dose distributions, planning CT, OOI segmentations and clinical features. A conventional NTCP model using oral cavity mean dose, parotid mean dose, and age served as reference. Attention maps were evaluated for the transformer-based DL model to quantify the model attention to specific regions of the head and neck area. In addition, two cropping approaches for the 3D data were compared.

RESULTS: The CNN and transformer DL models performed comparable to the reference NTCP model in the test set (Reference: AUC = 0.71; ResNet: AUC = 0.68; TransRP: AUC = 0.71), though calibration was best for the reference model. Shifting the crop improved DL performance and transformer attention focused on supraglottic and submandibular regions.

CONCLUSION: This study showed that the prediction of taste alteration can be achieved using DL models, particularly transformer-based models which, in contrast to CNNs, can account for global features of comprehensive 3D information of dose distribution, CT-images and organs-of-interest segmentations.

paper.title: The Importance of Nasal Airflow Distribution for Olfactory Function and Paranasal Sinus Ventilation: Insights From a Computational Fluid Dynamics Evaluation in Dupilumab-Treated CRSwNP Patients.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dupilumab is an established treatment for severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), leading to significant improvements in symptoms and olfactory function. However, objective data on how dupilumab modifies nasal airflow distribution and paranasal sinus ventilation are limited. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) allows detailed, quantitative evaluation of nasal airflow changes that cannot be assessed in vivo. This study aims to quantify changes in nasal airflow, olfactory cleft ventilation, and paranasal sinus patency after dupilumab treatment, and to explore their relationship with olfactory outcomes.

METHODS: This retrospective, single-center CFD study included 26 adult patients with type 2 CRSwNP treated with dupilumab for 6 months. Paired pre- and post-treatment CT scans (52 scans) were analyzed using registered CFD simulations. Total nasal airflow and airflow distribution across three nasal sections were quantified during inspiration and expiration. Olfactory function was assessed using the Sniffin' Sticks Identification Test (SSIT-16). Paranasal sinus patency was scored (0-16) and correlated with the Completion of Surgery Index (CoSI). Pre- and post-treatment differences were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and correlations with Spearman's rho.

RESULTS: After 6 months, total inspiratory airflow increased from 17.35 ± 6.70 to 22.30 ± 4.71 L/min (p = 0.003), while total expiratory airflow increased from 18.15 ± 6.51 to 21.86 ± 5.69 L/min (p = 0.025). The greatest relative airflow increase occurred in the olfactory cleft (+567% inspiratory). SSIT-16 scores increased from 4.7 ± 3.2 to 10.3 ± 2.7, and the change in inspiratory airflow within the olfactory section significantly correlated with the change in SSIT-16 score (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.028). Paranasal sinus patency increased by 7.5 points (p < 0.01), without a significant correlation with CoSI.

CONCLUSIONS: Dupilumab significantly improves nasal airflow and paranasal sinus ventilation in CRSwNP. Increased airflow in the olfactory cleft is associated with improved olfactory function, supporting a conductive component of smell loss in these patients.

paper.title: Colony isolation of odorant receptor-expressing insect sensor cells in hollow hydrogel microparticles for enhanced biohybrid sensor sensitivity.
paper.abstract: Cell-based biohybrid sensors using insect olfactory receptors (ORs) have emerged as promising sensing platforms for the selective and sensitive detection of biomarkers. A single sensor cell provides a weak signal, so the readout of most biohybrid sensors is the accumulated response of a whole population of cells. Response heterogeneity within engineered sensor cell populations can limit sensor sensitivity because low-responding cells dilute the bulk-averaged signal. Selecting highly responsive subclones could improve sensor sensitivity. However, most insect cell lines proliferate poorly at low cell density, making it challenging to obtain expandable colonies from a single insect cell. Here, we present a colony-isolation workflow for insect sensor cells using hollow hydrogel microparticles (PicoShells). Insect sensor cells were encapsulated in PicoShells at limiting dilutions to physically isolate one or a few cells. The encapsulated insect sensor cells were co-cultured with non-encapsulated support cells in the same suspension culture to promote colony formation. Individual colony-containing PicoShells were isolated and expanded into subclonal cell lines. Functional screening using a portable fluorescence detector and a microwell array identified a highly responsive subclone. In a human urine sample spiked with acetophenone, a candidate volatile biomarker of disease, this subclone showed an approximately 2.4-fold higher response sensitivity than the parental cell line, and the limit of detection was reduced from 1.56 ± 0.17 μM to 0.93 ± 0.22 μM for this subclone. These results indicate that colony isolation using PicoShells, combined with functional screening, provides a practical strategy for improving the sensitivity of insect cell biohybrid sensors.

paper.title: A Multimodal Integration Framework for Taste and Odor Prediction and Flavor Molecule Discovery.
paper.abstract: Data-driven molecular property prediction is increasingly used to accelerate molecular discovery and computer-aided design. In flavor science, accurate prediction of molecular taste and odor attributes could facilitate the screening and rational design of candidate flavor molecules. However, this task remains challenging because structure-flavor relationships are complex, single molecular representations may provide incomplete property-relevant information, and the available labels are highly imbalanced. To address these challenges, we implemented and evaluated Uni-Flavor, a multimodal prediction framework embedded in an integrated computational discovery workflow. Uni-Flavor combines three-dimensional molecular representations extracted from a LoRA-fine-tuned Uni-Mol2 model with stability-selected Mordred physicochemical descriptors through a dual-branch fusion architecture incorporating modality-specific projection, multiplicative late fusion, label-aware classification, and imbalance-aware optimization. Independent taste and odor models were trained separately under a common modeling and evaluation protocol, using curated datasets containing 17,202 taste molecules across six categories and 4,983 odor molecules across 138 labels. On held-out test sets, the taste model achieved an accuracy of 95.63% and an AUROC of 97.35%, an AUPRC of 82.05%, and an F1 score of 76.32%, whereas the corresponding values for the odor model were 96.03%, 89.97%, 38.00% and 36.94%. Branch-specific atom-level attribution analysis provided heuristic structural insights into the Uni-Mol2-derived component of the predictions by associating attribution patterns with specific molecular substructures. The trained models were subsequently used to screen approximately 670,000 natural products and coupled with a ScaffoldCAMD strategy for the constrained design of synthetic flavor candidates under chemical-validity, scaffold-assembly, and physicochemical-property constraints, followed by preliminary structural safety filtering. Molecular docking was further used to examine plausible receptor-ligand interactions and provide preliminary receptor-level support for selected candidates. This work presents a common multimodal modeling strategy that integrates three-dimensional molecular representations with physicochemical descriptors and is instantiated independently for multilabel taste and odor prediction. Although developed for flavor-related prediction, evaluation on the SIDER dataset provides preliminary cross-task evidence that the multimodal integration strategy can be applied to another imbalanced multilabel molecular property problem; broader transferability to other property domains remains to be established.

Although adjuvant-insecticide mixtures did not significantly impair learning ability, these adjuvants may impact sensory perception. Moving beyond mortality-based assessments and including behavioural assay to test sensory perception and learning ability is essential for gaining a more holistic understanding of pollinator health.

paper.title: Olfactory Training and Patient-Centered Outcomes Beyond Smell: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is associated with diminished quality of life (QOL), depressive symptoms, and cognitive decline, and emerging evidence suggests that olfactory training (OT) may mitigate both OD and its broader impacts. This review aims to systematically evaluate the effects of OT on QOL, depression, and cognitive outcomes.

METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published between 1990 and 2025. PRISMA guidelines were followed for study screening and data extraction. Studies evaluating the effects of OT on QOL, depressive symptoms, or cognitive function were included. Random-effects models were used to pool within-group standardized mean changes (SMC) and between-group standardized mean differences (SMD).

RESULTS: Fifty-one studies met inclusion criteria, with 19 included in quantitative synthesis. OT was associated with improvement in olfactory-specific QOL (Questionnaire of Olfactory Disorders [QOD] SMC = 1.29; 95% CI [0.04-2.55]). Among controlled trials, OT produced a significant advantage in QOD improvement over no-OT (QOD SMD = 0.40; 95% CI: 0.04-0.76). OT was associated with a modest improvement in global cognitive performance (Montreal Cognitive Assessment mean difference = 0.65; 95% CI [0.35, 0.94]), but no significant effect was observed on depressive symptoms (Beck Depression Inventory SMC = -0.20; 95% CI: [-0.55, 0.14]).

CONCLUSIONS: OT is associated with improved olfactory-specific QOL and cognitive benefits. These findings support the potential of OT as a low-cost intervention to support the multifaceted challenges experienced by individuals with OD, while highlighting the need for adequately powered studies to clarify its effectiveness for treating OD-associated depression.

paper.title: Olfactory combinatorial coding supports risk-reward decision-making in Caenorhabditis elegans.
paper.abstract: Olfactory-driven behaviors are essential for animal survival, but mechanisms for decoding olfactory inputs remain poorly understood. We have used whole-network Ca2+ imaging to study olfactory coding in Caenorhabditis elegans. We show that the odorant 1-octanol is encoded combinatorially in the periphery as both an attractant and a repellent. These inputs are integrated centrally, and their relative strengths determine the sensitivity and valence of the behavioral response through modulation of locomotory reversals and speed. The balance of these pathways also dictates the activity of the locomotory command interneurons, which control locomotory reversals. This balance serves as a regulatory node for response modulation, allowing C. elegans to weigh opportunities and hazards in its environment when formulating behavioral responses. Thus, an odorant can be encoded simultaneously as inputs of opposite valence, focusing attention on the integration of these inputs in determining perception, response, and plasticity.

paper.title: Acute Olfactory Hypersensitivity to Opium and Cannabis Following Naltrexone Administration: A Rare Case Report.
paper.abstract: Naltrexone, a long-acting opioid receptor antagonist, is commonly utilized to avert relapse in individuals with opioid or alcohol dependence. We present a rare case of a 16-year-old male with a history of cannabis usage who experienced acute episodes of respiratory distress after starting oral naltrexone (50 mg/day). These episodes were consistently triggered by the smell of opium or cannabis smoke, despite the patient's abstinence. The reactions were severe enough to necessitate multiple emergency medical procedures. The patient had a prior adverse reaction to morphine and a history of multiple drug allergies, suggesting a possible underlying sensitivity to opioid system modulation. The symptoms resolved after discontinuation of naltrexone. This case raises significant clinical and neurobiological concerns about the role of opioid antagonism in modifying olfactory and emotional processing. We propose that naltrexone-induced disinhibition in olfactory-limbic circuits may have contributed to heightened sensory gain and conditioned unpleasant reactions in a sensitized individual. More research is needed to understand the mechanisms driving this unusual yet important reaction.

paper.title: Clinicopathological Characteristics and Recurrence Patterns of Olfactory Neuroblastoma: A 15-Year Tertiary Center Case Series.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Olfactory neuroblastoma (ONB) is a rare malignant tumor of the sinonasal tract with heterogeneous clinical behavior and recurrence potential. Due to its low incidence, prognostic factors and optimal treatment strategies remain incompletely defined. The objective of this study was to describe the clinicopathological characteristics, treatment approaches, and recurrence patterns of ONB over a 15-year period at a tertiary referral center.

METHODS: A retrospective case series and literature review were performed. Medical records of nine patients with histologically confirmed ONB treated between 2007 and 2022 were reviewed. Demographic characteristics, presenting symptoms, imaging findings, Hyams histologic grade, treatment modalities, and follow-up outcomes were analyzed. Diagnosis in every case rested on characteristic morphology together with a full neuroendocrine immunohistochemical panel, and Hyams grade was assigned on the definitive resection specimen. Variables that were not uniformly documented across the 15-year archive-clinical stage, surgical margin status and the anatomical compartment of recurrence-were deliberately not imputed and are reported as unavailable.

RESULTS: Patients ranged in age from 18 to 61 years (mean 41.3 ± 12.4 years; median 42 years), with a male predominance (6/9, 66.7%). The most common presenting symptoms were nasal congestion, headache, and nasal mass. All patients underwent surgical resection with curative intent, predominantly through endoscopic endonasal approaches, followed by adjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Within a uniform, protocol-defined posttreatment observation window of 3 years (median follow-up 36 months), tumor recurrence occurred in 4 of 9 patients (44.4%), and 5 of 9 patients (55.6%) remained free of documented recurrence. Recurrence was observed across different Hyams grades, including grade I tumors, without a statistically significant association between histologic grade, age, or gender and recurrence.

CONCLUSIONS: ONB demonstrates variable clinical presentation and recurrence patterns, even following multimodal treatment. Histologic grade alone may not reliably predict recurrence in small cohorts. Recurrence despite low-grade histology and uniformly administered chemoradiotherapy supports grade-, stage-, and margin-adapted rather than uniform adjuvant strategies, and structured surveillance continued well beyond 5 years.

paper.title: Duration of Olfactory Loss and Steroid Responsiveness as Predictors of Treatment Response to Dupilumab in Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Olfactory dysfunction affects 60%-80% of patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). Dupilumab improves olfactory outcomes in CRSwNP, but the degree of improvement varies among patients. This study examined whether duration of olfactory loss, steroid responsiveness, and baseline smell fluctuation are associated with dupilumab treatment response.

METHODS: CRSwNP patients initiating dupilumab were enrolled in a single-arm, prospective study. Duration of olfactory loss, steroid responsiveness, and baseline smell fluctuation were recorded. Olfactory testing using Sniffin' Sticks (threshold, discrimination, identification, and composite TDI score) and patient-reported smell ability were documented at baseline and after 12 weeks of dupilumab. The relationship between these clinical features and olfactory outcomes was analyzed.

RESULTS: Patients who reported a shorter duration of olfactory loss had greater TDI improvement (R2 = 0.089, p = 0.02) after dupilumab. Steroid-responsive patients showed higher change scores across several measures, including patient-reported olfaction and smell identification scores, although there was no overall difference in TDI improvement. Patients reporting baseline smell fluctuation had higher TDI scores throughout treatment but showed similar magnitude of change.

CONCLUSIONS: Duration of olfactory loss is associated with dupilumab treatment response in CRSwNP, with a 10-year threshold identifying patients less likely to achieve clinically meaningful improvement. Steroid responsiveness provides additional prognostic value. These readily available clinical features can guide patient counseling and treatment expectations.

paper.title: Malodorous compound production driven by microbial succession during Chinese cabbage decomposition.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chinese cabbage is one of the most widely consumed vegetables in China. However, malodorous compounds generated from the decomposition of discarded leaves during harvest and distribution have become a significant environmental concern. This study aimed to identify the key odor compounds produced during Chinese cabbage decompostion and to characterize their associations with microbial community dynamics.

RESULTS: Physicochemical monitoring showed declining total solids and sugars, rising soluble protein, and fluctuating total nitrogen. Gas chromatography-olfactometry-mass spectrometry (GC-O-MS) identified dimethyl disulfide and dimethyl trisulfide as early dominant odorants. The content of dimethyl disulfide increased from 0.53 to 59.29 μg/kg by day 3, while dimethyl trisulfide peaked at 14.08 μg/kg on day 3 and then became undetectable. Indole accumulated to 9.82 μg/kg by day 5 and persisted thereafter, becoming the major malodorous compound in mid-to-late stages. Full-length 16S/ITS sequencing revealed distinct bacterial and fungal succession, with Alcaligenes faecalis dominating (42.25%) at day 11 and Geotrichum silvicola and Candida tropicalis prevailing among fungi. Spearman correlation suggested associations between specific taxa and key odorants. Screening and validation confirmed that Rhodotorula mucilaginosa and Yarrowia lipolytica removed > 99.7% of indole.

CONCLUSION: Dimethyl disulfide, dimethyl trisulfide, and indole are the principal odor compounds during Chinese cabbage decomposition, with indole dominating the later stages. Microbial succession drives the temporal shift in odor profiles. Rhodotorula mucilaginosa and Yarrowia lipolytica were validated as highly effective indole-degrading agents, highlighting their potential for biological odor mitigation during cabbage decomposition, although their capacity for sulfur-compound removal remains limited. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

paper.title: The Microbiome-Metabolokine-Adipokine Axis in Insulin Resistance: Adaptive and Maladaptive FGF21-GDF15 Signaling.
paper.abstract: Insulin resistance emerges from disturbances in interorgan metabolic communication in which nutrient exposure, microbial metabolism, and host endocrine responses interact across multiple metabolic compartments. This state-of-the-art review proposes a revised Microbiome-Metabolokine-Adipokine (MMA) Axis as a focused framework linking gut microbial metabolic signals with enteroendocrine, hepatic, and adipose responses and the stress-responsive metabolokines fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15). Microbiome-derived and microbiome-modified signals, including short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, branched-chain amino acid-related metabolites, tryptophan-derived metabolites, and microbial inflammatory products, can influence intestinal receptor signaling, incretin secretion, hepatic nutrient sensing, adipose lipid buffering, and systemic insulin sensitivity. Within this network, FGF21 and GDF15 are positioned as distinct but complementary adaptive endocrine signals rather than components of a fixed sequential pathway: FGF21 predominantly coordinates responses to nutrient and metabolic stress, whereas GDF15 communicates broader cellular stress through GFRAL-RET-dependent regulation of nutrient intake and energy balance. Importantly, persistent elevation of either metabolokine during insulin-resistant states should not automatically be interpreted as endocrine resistance or maladaptation. We instead propose that progression toward insulin resistance reflects a context-dependent mismatch between increasing metabolic stress and the capacity of integrated endocrine responses to maintain metabolic flexibility and substrate homeostasis. Current evidence strongly supports individual microbiome-metabolite, enteroendocrine, hepatic, adipose, FGF21, and GDF15 signaling modules, but a direct causal microbiome-FGF21-GDF15 sequence has not been established in humans. The revised MMA Axis therefore provides a testable framework for defining how microbiome-derived metabolic signals interface with host endocrine adaptation during the development of insulin resistance.

paper.title: Compartment-specific redox modulation in migraine with aura: a systematic review of context-dependent mechanisms.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preventive therapies for migraine with aura (MA) remain suboptimal, with 37-54% of patients failing to achieve a >50% reduction in migraine days despite calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-targeted therapies, while broad-spectrum antioxidants show inconsistent benefits. This gap suggests that indiscriminate reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging is insufficient, but emerging evidence indicates that ROS function as compartment-specific signaling molecules rather than uniform toxins. Whether this compartment-specific redox modulation occurs within the cortical spreading depression (CSD) cascade and contributes to the limited efficacy of antioxidant therapies remains unclear. We synthesized preclinical evidence to characterize CSD-redox interactions and identify the translational gap limiting precision strategies for MA.

METHODS: We systematically searched five databases through June 2025 following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Risk of bias was assessed using the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) risk-of-bias tool. Given the anticipated heterogeneity, a qualitative synthesis was conducted.

RESULTS: Thirteen studies (594 animals, 85% male) were included. CSD-evoked ROS were associated with transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1)/CGRP signaling and oxidative wavefront propagation. Under bioenergetic stress, ROS accumulation was associated with metabolic collapse, which may trigger CSD onset. Microglial M1-like polarization was associated with reduced CSD thresholds. High-dose melatonin accelerated CSD propagation without improving oxidative markers, suggesting limitations of global antioxidant strategies rather than invalidation of the redox framework. Cell-specific protective mechanisms emerged through microglial M2a-like polarization and compartment-specific stabilization of insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1).

CONCLUSION: CSD-redox interactions represent a context-dependent reciprocal axis. Clinical failure of broad-spectrum scavengers may reflect disruption of oxidative eustress. Modulators of microglial M2a-like phenotype and compartment-specific bioenergetic stabilizers should be prioritized for future drug development. Intranasal IGF-1 represents a potentially translatable strategy for attenuating trigeminal CGRP release and oxidative markers, although this requires validation in female cohorts and assessment of sex-specific effects.

paper.title: Mapping the Research Landscape and Global Trends: A Bibliometric Analysis of Event-related Potential in Alzheimer's Disease.
paper.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: There is an urgent need for objective biomarkers to facilitate early diagnosis and dynamic monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Event-Related Potential (ERP), as a neuroelectrophysiological technique with high temporal resolution, shows great promise in addressing this demand. However, the macro-level developmental trajectory, research status, and frontier directions within this field remain to be systematically elucidated. This study employs bibliometric methods to delineate the development trends, knowledge structures, and research frontiers of ERP applications in AD, thereby offering a novel perspective for early diagnosis, dynamic monitoring, and efficacy assessment.

METHOD: Publications related to ERP and AD were retrieved and screened from the Web of Science Core Collection. A comprehensive quantitative and visual analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel, CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the bibliometrix package in R. The analysis covered publication trends, national/institutional collaboration networks, author co-occurrence, core journals, reference and keyword co-occurrence, and clustering.

RESULTS: The number of annual publications in this field continued to grow. The United States, China, and Italy were the most productive countries, whereas the cooperation network among institutions and authors was decentralized. Keyword clustering identified six major research topics: P300/N200, Mismatch Negativity (MMN), N170, N400, Olfactory Event-Related Potential (OERP), and Electroencephalography (EEG).

DISCUSSION: An analysis of the global research landscape reveals that ERP research has developed from an exploratory tool in the field of AD to an active research field of neuroscience. Journal and citation analysis indicate that the field has distinct clinical problem-driven features; keyword cluster analysis revealed six major themes corresponding to classical cognitive assessment, early sensory memory, and social cognition. Thematic analysis revealed that MMN and other ERP components that are sensitive to early abnormalities may become future research hotspots; however, the overall cooperation in this field still shows a certain degree of geographical concentration and institutional dispersion. In the future, it is necessary to build a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network, establish a standardized ERP evaluation scheme, and embed it throughout the entire process of early identification, staging, and monitoring of the effect of intervention in AD.

CONCLUSION: This research systematically presents the current state of research, hotspots, and evolutionary trends in ERP in the field of AD. The results suggest that in the future, a closer international and interdisciplinary cooperation network and further prospective clinical validation are needed to clarify the diagnostic performance and practical application value of ERP, thereby promoting its clinical application.

Strong correlations between dorsal cranial length and both endocast and labyrinthine parameters suggest that sensory-related neuroanatomical morphology in C. siamensis follows a consistent ontogenetic scaling pattern. BACKGROUND: Endometriosis (EM) is a multifactorial, estrogen-dependent inflammatory disease characterized by high clinical variability. Growing evidence is highlighting the role of gut microbiome dysbiosis in EM pathophysiology; however, associations between microbiome, symptom severity, and host genetics remain poorly characterized. Extra-oral taste receptor genes (TGs), expressed in both the gastrointestinal and female reproductive systems, may represent novel mediators of gut-reproductive tract axis crosstalk.

METHODS: A total of 50 women with surgically confirmed EM were deeply clinically characterized, including the evaluation of EM-symptoms and their severity. Microbiome profiles were obtained by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of rectal swabs. Genetic variants within four TGs (TAS2R3, TAS2R4, TAS2R5, and TAS2R14) were assessed using SNP-array genotyping. Microbiome composition was investigated through the evaluation of alpha and beta diversity, as well as enterotype classification analyses. Associations between EM-related features, bacterial taxa and TG-SNPs were investigated using regression models.

RESULTS: Three distinct gut microbiome community types were identified, dominated by Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Escherichia-Shigella. While microbiome composition did not differ significantly across EM stages, beta diversity was associated with dysmenorrhea (R2 = 0.13) and disease stage (R2 = 0.12). Regarding TGs, SNPs within TAS2R14 gene showed significant associations with alpha and beta diversity indices. Reduced abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa, including members of the Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae families, was associated with dysmenorrhea, whereas increased abundance of Prevotella and Mobiluncus with dysuria and infertility, respectively. Finally, an increased premenstrual pain severity was associated with a reduced relative abundance of taxa within the order Burkholderiales (β = -2.265) and the family Sutterellaceae (β = -1.563); high postmenstrual pain severity was associated with a lower abundance of Bifidobacteriales (β = -4.932) and Bifidobacteriaceae (β = -4.134).

CONCLUSION: This case-only study elucidated the complex relationship between gut microbiome composition, EM-related symptoms, and host genetic variation. In particular, extra-oral taste receptor genes emerged as novel risk factors to host-microbiome interactions, supporting their potential role in the microbiota-endometriosis axis and opening new perspectives on EM pathogenesis.

paper.title: Post-Vaccination Chemosensory Dysfunction: Changes Following SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination in a Global Study.
paper.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess post-vaccination changes in chemosensory function among individuals with and without COVID-19-related chemosensory impairment.

METHODS: In this global, multilingual online survey, participants reported vaccination status, vaccine side effects, and changes in smell and taste before and after each vaccine dose. Responses were collected between May 2022 and August 2023 through convenience sampling. Of 2955 responses, 1352 were included after applying exclusion criteria.

RESULTS: Pfizer-BioNTech accounted for 46.2% of vaccine doses, followed by Sputnik V (16.3%), Moderna (15.4%), AstraZeneca (8.9%), and Sinopharm (7.4%). More than 90% of participants reported no change in general smell or taste following vaccination, regardless of pre-existing chemosensory impairment. Among participants with qualitative chemosensory distortions, improvement was reported by 11%-18% for parosmia, 20%-29% for phantosmia, and 12%-21% for distorted taste, depending on vaccine dose, whereas worsening was reported by 3% or fewer. Side effects varied by vaccine type and were more frequent among individuals reporting worsened chemosensory symptoms.

CONCLUSION: Most participants reported stable smell and taste perception following vaccination. A subset of individuals with qualitative chemosensory distortions reported improvement, while worsening was uncommon.

paper.title: Decoding channel pore dynamics mechanism in Anopheles gambiae Orco homotetramer.
paper.abstract:
MOTIVATION: Insect odorant receptors (iORs) essential for olfaction function as 7-transmembrane-domain (7TM) ion channels. iORs form tetrameric complexes that include a highly conserved odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco). Functional Orco homotetramers have also known to form ex vivo. Blocking Orco ex vivo and in vivo disrupts olfactory signalling, making it a promising target for functional intervention. Understanding its gating behaviour is critical for developing strategies to disrupt odour-guided behaviours in disease-vector insects. Thus, insights into the dynamic gating of the Anopheles gambiae Orco have implications on the rational design of vector-control strategies against malaria. We studied molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on homotetrameric AgamOrco models generated using template-based modelling (TBM) and AlphaFold3 (AF3), to investigate ligand-dependent pore dynamics. Agonist and antagonist bound systems were analysed to understand the ligand-dependent gating.

RESULTS: Our results show that apo and antagonistic IPC-bound AgamOrco homotetramer models remain in a stable, closed, and non-conductive state across both models. TBM, but not AF3, successfully captures agonistic VUAA1-induced activation, consistent with experimental observations, exhibiting asymmetric pore widening and conformational changes. Antagonist displacement simulations confirm IPC-mediated pore closure. Overall, the TBM AgamOrco model provides a reliable framework for structure-guided discovery of novel agents for control of insect pests and vector diseases.

paper.title: Efficacy and safety of middle turbinate resection versus preservation during endoscopic sinus surgery in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a common inflammatory disease that significantly impairs quality of life. When symptoms persist despite medical therapy, endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) is performed. During ESS, whether to resect or preserve the middle turbinate remains controversial: resection may improve access and reduce postoperative obstruction, while preservation maintains anatomy and may support normal healing and airflow. Evidence comparing both approaches is limited and inconsistent, so their relative efficacy and safety remain unclear.

METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across various databases until January 2026 to identify relevant studies. The quality was assessed using the ROB2 and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) tools and the analysis was performed using R software.

RESULTS: The search identified 4,265 records; after screening and full-text assessment, 31 studies were included. Compared with preservation, middle turbinate resection showed a statistically significant improvement in Lund-Kennedy endoscopic score (MD = - 0.58), while symptom improvement measured by SNOT showed no significant difference. Resection significantly reduced postoperative adhesion/synechiae (RR = 0.35) and sinus ostium restenosis (RR = 0.41). For secondary outcomes, olfaction and POSE scores did not differ significantly between groups, and crustation and middle meatal antrostomy patency were not significantly different. Postoperative bleeding risk was higher with resection (RR = 2.24), whereas lateralization (RR = 0.29) and polyp recurrence (RR = 0.58) were lower with resection.

CONCLUSION: Middle turbinate resection during ESS for CRS appears to improve postoperative endoscopic healing and patency-related outcomes (including reduced synechiae and ostial restenosis), but it does not confer a consistent advantage in patient-reported symptoms and is associated with a higher risk of postoperative bleeding; therefore, MT management should be individualized and anatomy-/risk-guided rather than routine.

paper.title: Astrocytic glutamate transporter loss drives chemoreflex hyperactivity and cardiorespiratory dysfunction in a heart failure model.
paper.abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Breathing instability and exaggerated chemoreflex activation contribute to adverse HF outcomes, yet the central mechanisms linking respiratory control to cardiac dysfunction remain poorly defined. The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is a key brainstem chemosensory region regulating ventilatory and autonomic output, but whether glial dysfunction within this circuit contributes to HF pathophysiology is unknown. We hypothesized that loss of astrocytic glutamate transporter 1 (GLT-1) in the RTN disrupts glutamate homeostasis, producing chemoreflex hyperactivity and cardiorespiratory dysfunction in HF. In a rat model of nonischemic HF, reduced astrocytic GLT-1 expression in the RTN was accompanied by extracellular glutamate accumulation and heightened excitability of chemosensitive neurons. These changes were associated with exaggerated central chemoreflex responses, breathing instability, autonomic imbalance, and impaired cardiac function. Astrocyte-specific GLT-1 restoration normalized RTN glutamate levels, reduced central chemoreceptor neuron hyperexcitability, stabilized breathing, and improved cardiac performance. Systemic riluzole, an FDA-approved glutamate-modulating drug, similarly reduced RTN glutamate accumulation and attenuated chemoreflex-driven respiratory instability. These findings identify loss of astrocytic GLT-1-mediated glutamate homeostasis in the RTN as a mechanism contributing to cardiorespiratory dysfunction in HF and support pharmacological targeting of brainstem glutamate homeostasis as a therapeutic strategy requiring further investigation.

paper.title: Dyspnea during resting breathing and carbon dioxide rebreathing in adult patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.
paper.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is an ultra-rare genetic disorder caused by PHOX2B mutations. Patients lack central CO2 chemosensitivity and require ventilatory support during sleep. Children with CCHS have been reported to lack CO2-induced air hunger, but respiratory sensations and dyspnea have not been characterized in adults.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Do genetically characterized adult CCHS patients experience respiratory sensations and dyspnea during unassisted resting breathing and CO2 rebreathing, and along which dimensions?

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: This was a prospective controlled observational study conducted on a convenience sample derived from a national cohort of an ultrarare disease. Thirteen adult CCHS patients carrying PHOX2B mutations underwent Multidimensional Dyspnea Profile (MDP) assessment during unassisted resting breathing and at the end of CO2 rebreathing. Healthy controls were studied under the same conditions.

RESULTS: Before the study, none of the patients had spontaneously reported dyspnea or bothersome respiratory sensations. When prompted with the MDP during resting breathing, 9/13 patients described breathing unpleasantness (non-zero MDP-A1) versus 0/18 controls (p < 0.0001), and 12/13 fulfilled criteria for dyspnea defined as breathing awareness associated with negative affect. During CO2 rebreathing, ventilatory responses remained profoundly blunted, yet breathing unpleasantness increased. Compared with controls, patients had lower sensory and affective ratings, with less frequent air hunger (p = 0.0108). MDP ratings did not correlate with ventilatory response to CO2 or genotype.

INTERPRETATION: Adult CCHS patients can experience conscious unpleasant breathing awareness at rest and retain a perceptual response to CO2 despite abolished or nearly abolished central chemosensitivity. These findings suggest respiratory interoceptive pathways beyond canonical brainstem chemosensitive circuits and support active multidimensional assessment of dyspnea in adult CCHS patients.

paper.title: Adverse oral effects of GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonists: a scoping review protocol.
paper.abstract:
ABSTRACT: 

INTRODUCTION: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual incretin receptor agonists such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are increasingly being prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity due to their efficacy in glycaemic control, weight loss and cardiovascular risk reduction. Emerging pharmacovigilance data suggest potential oral adverse effects, including xerostomia, dysgeusia, oral hypoesthesia and throat discomfort. Therefore, alterations in salivary function may compromise oral homeostasis and increase susceptibility to dental caries, periodontal inflammation and mucosal irritation. Additionally, metabolic and inflammatory changes mediated by GLP-1 and GIP may indirectly affect oral tissues. However, current evidence remains limited and inconsistently reported. Further research is needed to investigate the prevalence, underlying mechanisms and clinical significance of oral manifestations associated with GLP-1RA and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist medications, as well as to explore the need for individualised management strategies and more frequent monitoring for patients receiving these therapies.

METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This protocol describes the methodology for a future scoping review to be conducted in accordance with the JBI reporting guidelines. Studies addressing incretin-based medications and their implications for oral health will be eligible for inclusion in the review, with no restrictions on language or publication date. The following databases will be searched: Cochrane, LILACS, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science. Additional literature will be identified through Google Scholar and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global. The snowballing technique and consultation with experts in the field will be used to identify additional relevant studies. The findings will be presented through a narrative synthesis, supported by tables, graphs and maps. When data are available, exploratory comparisons will be performed according to therapeutic indication (type 2 diabetes or obesity) and pharmacological class (GLP-1RAs and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonists), with particular attention to tirzepatide and other incretin-based agents, to explore potential differences in reported oral manifestations. In particular, studies involving different GLP-1RA and GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonists agents (eg, semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide) may be compared to explore potential differences in reported oral manifestations. These comparisons will be conducted descriptively, considering variations in dosage, treatment duration and pharmacological class when such information is reported.

REGISTRATION DETAILS: This protocol has been registered prospectively on the Open Science Framework (DOI:10.17605/OSF.IO/NWTCS).

ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This scoping review protocol does not require ethics approval, as it only describes the methodological aspects of a future scoping review and uses secondary data from previously published studies. The findings of the review will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presentations at scientific conferences. As this study is a protocol for a scoping review and does not involve human participants or identifiable data, ethics committee approval was not required.

paper.title: Integrative systematics reveal an unusual species of pedunculate ground beetles lacking fossorial legs from Late Cretaceous Kachin amber (Coleoptera: Carabidae: Scaritinae).
paper.abstract:
CONTEXT: The subfamily Scaritinae (Coleoptera: Carabidae) is a speciose, cosmopolitan group of ground beetles characterised by a pedunculate body form and modified fossorial forelegs, adaptations associated with a burrowing lifestyle in soil or sandy substrates. The fossil record of Scaritinae is scarce and only one Mesozoic species has been described up to the present.

AIMS: A new genus and species of scaritine ground beetles is described from Late Cretaceous amber in northern Myanmar. Its phylogenetic relationship with extant lineages of Scaritinae was investigated and divergence times among lineages of Scaritinae were estimated. Its palaeoecology is also discussed from the perspective of morphological adaptation.

TAXON: A Late Cretaceous pedunculate ground beetle (Insecta: Coleoptera: Carabidae: Scaritinae), Cretoscarites burmanicus gen. et sp. nov., aligns well with extant Scaritinae, yet it lacks the fossorial legs typically seen in modern scaritines.

METHODS: Its relationship with extant Scaritinae was investigated based on two datasets using maximum parsimony, Bayesian inference and maximum likelihood: (i) 55 morphological characters belonging to 16 taxa (representing 6 of the 7 tribes and 13 of the 20 subtribes of modern Scaritinae); and (ii) a combined morphological and molecular dataset for 16 taxa, comprising a partitioned alignment of 2772 bp from COI and 18S sequences of seven taxa, representing 5 tribes and 6 subtribes. Divergence times within Scaritinae were estimated in a Bayesian tip-dating framework based on both datasets under a relaxed clock.

KEY RESULTS: Phylogenetic analyses using various approaches and datasets consistently placed Cretoscarites burmanicus within Scaritini. Among Scaritini, the nominal subtribe was recovered as the most likely closest relative of Cretoscarites burmanicus. Results indicate that Scaritinae originated in the Middle Jurassic (ca. 167-168 Mya) and the major lineages started to differentiate during the Cretaceous. The overall body form and small eye size suggest that it was likely a nocturnal, olfactory-tactile hunter inhabiting restricted or confined environments, whereas its simple, unmodified forelegs indicate a non-fossorial lifestyle.

CONCLUSIONS: The newly described scaritine ground beetle from Kachin amber can be confidently assigned to Scaritini based on our integrative phylogenetic approach. This finding represents the oldest documented occurrence (ca. 99 Mya) of this tribe to date and its unique forelegs suggest that the lifestyles of Scaritinae may have been more diverse in their early evolution than they are today. ZooBank LSID: urn:lsid:zoobank.org:pub:7E489EEA-A5A2-422B-B3EA-45B9FF3600D9.
